title: People chose to repeat the longer of two painful experiences
body: In a 1993 experiment, volunteers held a hand in painfully cold 14 °C water for 60 seconds. In a second trial they did the same, then kept the hand in for 30 more seconds while the water warmed slightly, to 15 °C. Asked which trial to repeat, most picked the longer one. Daniel Kahneman and his colleagues called this the **peak–end rule**: we remember an experience by its most intense moment and by how it ended, and largely forget how long it lasted.

left.label: Trial A
left.text: 60 seconds with a hand in 14 °C water.

right.label: Trial B
right.text: The same 60 seconds, plus 30 more at a slightly warmer 15 °C. More pain in total, but a gentler ending.

slides.heading: Memory is not a sum
slides.text: The remembering self doesn’t add up every second. It samples the peak and the ending, and the length barely registers, a quirk Kahneman called duration neglect. Trial B’s milder last half-minute made the whole memory feel better.

slides.heading: Colonoscopies and holidays
slides.text: In a 1996 study, patients rated a colonoscopy by its worst moment and its final minutes, not by how long it took. The lesson travels: a trip, a meal or a meeting is judged by its best moment and its ending, so end things well.
